rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3; own field experiment in a Fuji apple orchard (Prosser, WA, 2013) comparing seven automatic scheduling algorithms in a randomized complete block design with three replications, reporting applied water (Table 2), soil water deficit and stem water potential (Fig. 7).
rows.notes: The study reports no result on crop production: Section 3.2 states that because the trees were in an alternate bearing year no quantitative fruit yield information was collected, and the Conclusions defer yield and fruit quality effects to future studies. What it does show is that automatic weather- and plant-based scheduling (WB, TTT, CWSI) applied about 30% of conventional water while keeping stem water potential in the non-stressed range and soil water deficit below MAD; this is a precondition (water-status maintenance) rather than evidence of sustainable production. Only qualitative observations of fruit size/shoot growth are given, and these show harm under soil-based algorithms, not a production gain.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field trial. Q2: Section 3.1 and Table 2; the SOIL treatment (Watermark granular matrix sensor with -30/-80 kPa wet/dry thresholds) applied the lowest total water, 214 mm, i.e. 53% of the neutron-probe reference and 16% of conventional practice, significantly less than all other treatments. Q4: Fig. 6 and Section 3.1; the study reports the soil water potential readings from the Watermark sensors in the SOIL and SL+WB plots, which stayed within 0 to -80 kPa and thus rarely triggered irrigation, and attributes the under-application to sensors monitoring a limited soil volume, lack of calibration and heterogeneous wetting under drip. Q7: Section 3.3 (and Table 4); authors state from their results that site-specific calibration of individual sensors, a larger number of sensors, or combined tension and content sensing appears necessary for the soil-based method to work reliably. Q8: Section 2.4.2 (sensors not field-calibrated, one sensor per plot), Section 3.1 (limited soil volume monitored, single predefined thresholds), Abstract/Conclusions (preliminary, single-season evaluation). Q9: Table 2 reports the standard error of the mean for applied water (SOIL: 32 mm; SL+WB: 43 mm).
rows.notes: Applied water was measured by one method (valve timing/flow accounting), so no triangulation. Single site, single crop, single season; plots of 18 trees within one orchard, no larger scale. The water decrease came with under-irrigation; the review's description of tensiometers differs slightly from the Watermark granular matrix sensors used, but both measure soil matric potential thresholds, so the technology matches.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field trial. Q2: Section 3.1 and 3.2 and Abstract; the SOIL and SL+WB (soil tension threshold) treatments produced tangible under-irrigation with leaf drop, loss of turgidity, reduced shoot and foliage growth, shorter trees, and apples noticeably smaller than CNTRL that never ripened (observational field inspections). Q4: Table 2 and Fig. 6; the intermediate under-irrigation is quantified (214 and 273 mm applied versus 401 mm for the neutron-probe reference) and the controlling soil water potential readings are reported. Q7: Section 3.3 and Table 4; the authors state that site-specific sensor calibration, more sensors or combined potential/content sensing appear necessary for the soil-based approach to deliver enough water and avoid stress. Q8: Section 3.2 explicitly states that no quantitative fruit yield data were collected because the trees were in an alternate bearing year, so only observations are available; Section 2.4.2 notes sensors were not calibrated; Conclusions call the results preliminary.
rows.notes: The harm to fruit size/quality and growth is established only by qualitative visual observation; stem water potential and neutron-probe soil water were not measured in the SOIL plots, and the Watermark readings themselves did not indicate stress, so there is no second independent method. No dispersion measure accompanies the fruit/growth observations (SE is given only for applied water). Single site, crop and season.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a single-season (2013), single-orchard field comparison of seven automatic irrigation scheduling algorithms for drip-irrigated Fuji apples near Prosser, WA; quantitative outcomes are applied water (Table 2 with SE), soil water deficit and stem water potential for CWSI/TTT/NP plots, and Watermark readings for SOIL/SL+WB plots; no yield data were collected.
